questions.prompt: The histogram shows household incomes in a town. Is a normal model appropriate?

choices.text: No: the distribution is strongly skewed right, not symmetric and mound-shaped.

questions.prompt: A spinner is claimed to land on each of 4 colors equally often. In 400 spins the counts are 98, 105, 97, 100. Are the results consistent with the claim?
questions.prompt_markup: A spinner is claimed to land on each of 4 colors equally often. In 400 spins the counts are 98, 105, 97, 100. Are the results consistent with the claim?

choices.text: Yes: each count is close to the expected 100.
No: the counts are not all exactly 100.
No: 105 proves the spinner favors one color.
Yes: any 4 counts adding to 400 are consistent.

questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: A model says a coin is fair. In 50 flips there were 34 heads. In 200 simulated runs of 50 fair flips, 3 runs had 34 or more heads. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. What do you conclude?
questions.prompt_markup: A model says a coin is fair. In 50 flips there were 34 heads. In 200 simulated runs of 50 fair flips, 3 runs had 34 or more heads. Use 5% as the cutoff for unusual. What do you conclude?

choices.text: 1.5% is not unusual, so the data show that the fair-coin model fits.
1.5% < 5%: unusual for a fair coin, so evidence against the model.
No simulated run had exactly 34 heads, so a fair coin has probability 0 of giving 34.
1.5% < 5%: this proves the coin is unfair.

questions.correct_answer: 1.5% < 5%: unusual for a fair coin, so evidence against the model.
questions.grading_note: 3/200 = 1.5%. Evidence is not proof, and a rare result is not impossible.

questions.prompt: How does judging a normal model for a data set differ from judging a probability model with a simulation?
questions.prompt_markup: How does judging a normal model for a data set differ from judging a probability model with a simulation?

choices.text: Both check whether the data form a bell curve; the simulation just repeats the same comparison many more times.
Both compare the sample mean with the population mean and ignore the shape of the data and the simulation.
The first uses many simulated runs of the model; the second only compares the shape of the histogram with a bell curve.
The first compares the shape of the data with a normal curve; the second asks whether an observed result is unusual among simulated results.

questions.correct_answer: The first compares the shape of the data with a normal curve; the second asks whether an observed result is unusual among simulated results.
questions.grading_note: Shape check versus how-unusual check. The others swap the two methods, describe both as the same shape check, or describe a comparison of means that neither method makes.
